stories.headline: STOCKS RIP HIGHER AS IRAN DE-ESCALATION HOPES CRUSH OIL AND EASE INFLATION FEARS
stories.body: The S&P 500 jumped 1.49% to 7,765 and the Nasdaq 100 surged 2.83% to 30,482 to open the week, with chip stocks (Intel, AMD, ARM) leading as diplomatic progress on Iran drove crude sharply lower and eased near-term inflation worries.
stories.explain: Equities are valued as the present value of future cash flows discounted by expected rates, so anything that lowers the inflation path lowers the rate path the market expects the Fed to hold, which lifts valuations today. Falling oil does double duty here: it directly cools the inflation numbers that would otherwise justify more Fed tightening, and it lowers input costs for the broad economy, both of which flow straight into a higher present value for stocks, especially longer-duration growth names like the mega-cap chip stocks that led the rally.

stories.headline: WTI SINKS TO $92, BRENT BREAKS BELOW $100 AS U.S.-IRAN TALKS ADVANCE
stories.body: WTI crude fell 2.18% to roughly $92 a barrel and Brent dropped below $100 for a fourth straight losing session, as diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the Iran standoff progressed and tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz held up despite earlier disruption fears.
stories.explain: Oil carries a geopolitical risk premium whenever a major producing region faces conflict risk, because traders price in the probability-weighted chance that supply gets disrupted, not just current flows. When diplomacy credibly lowers that probability, the premium unwinds fast even though actual barrels moving through the Strait of Hormuz haven't changed — the four-session slide reflects the market repricing tail risk down, not a shift in physical supply and demand.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 4.96% AS TRADERS TRIM BETS ON MORE FED HIKES
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped about 3 bps to 4.96%, pulling back from last week's push above 5%, as today's oil-driven relief in the inflation outlook led traders to modestly scale back expectations for additional hikes beyond the Fed's 25-bp move last week to 3.75%-4.00%.
stories.explain: The 10-year yield prices in the market's expected average path of short-term rates plus a term premium, so when incoming data suggests the Fed has less inflation to fight, the expected path of future hikes gets revised down and the yield falls even without any new Fed statement. Today's move shows bond traders reading the oil selloff as disinflationary enough to soften, if not reverse, last week's hawkish repricing that had pushed the 10-year above 5% in the first place.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS MODESTLY TO $4,390 AS SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND FADES WITH OIL SELLOFF
stories.body: Gold eased 0.13% to about $4,390 an ounce, giving back a sliver of its recent run as easing Middle East tensions reduced safe-haven demand, even though the dollar and nominal yields moved in offsetting directions today.
stories.explain: Gold's price responds to real (inflation-adjusted) yields and to geopolitical risk demand, not to nominal yields alone, so it can drift lower even on a day when nominal yields also fall, if the geopolitical risk premium embedded in gold shrinks faster than real yields do. Today's modest pullback reflects the same de-escalation story hitting oil: less tail-risk pricing, marginally less appetite for a pure safe-haven hedge, even with the broader inflation backdrop still supportive of gold near record levels.

stories.headline: DOLLAR TICKS UP TO 100.43 AS FED'S HAWKISH TILT KEEPS RATE-DIFFERENTIAL SUPPORT INTACT
stories.body: The DXY rose 0.12% to 100.43, extending a run that has the dollar up roughly 3% over the past 12 months, as last week's Fed hike and signal of at least one more increase this year keeps U.S. rate differentials wide versus other major economies.
stories.explain: A currency's level reflects the market's expected interest-rate gap against peer central banks over the relevant horizon, so a hawkish Fed that is still signaling further hikes supports the dollar even on a day when U.S. yields themselves eased slightly. The dollar's gain and the Treasury yield's dip aren't contradictory: the yield move reflects a slightly lower expected hike path at the margin, while the dollar's strength reflects that the U.S. still offers a wider rate advantage than most other major economies, hawkish-tilt intact.

stories.headline: NC STATE TAPS JUSTIN GAINEY AS NEW COACH WHILE TEXAS TECH ELIGIBILITY CASE HEADS TO COURT
stories.body: NC State hired longtime Rick Barnes assistant Justin Gainey as head coach after Will Wade departed for LSU, and a court hearing today over Texas Tech guard Darrion Williams' eligibility is testing rosters just as college basketball's first official practices open nationwide.

stories.headline: PISTONS HOLD LINE ON JALEN DUREN OFFER AS KINGS INTEREST SURFACES AHEAD OF CAMP
stories.body: Detroit is still declining to raise its roughly $190 million extension offer to center Jalen Duren, who is seeking $200 million-plus, with the Sacramento Kings reportedly making an offer the Pistons have so far rebuffed as training camp approaches in about two weeks.

stories.headline: FALCONS NAME PENIX STARTER FOR WEEK 3 AS BEARS' CALEB WILLIAMS GOES WEEK-TO-WEEK
stories.body: Atlanta confirmed Michael Penix Jr. will start at quarterback in Week 3 against Green Bay, while Chicago's Caleb Williams is considered week-to-week with a hamstring injury ahead of a Monday night matchup with Philadelphia, and Washington's Jayden Daniels is seeking outside opinions on his elbow with Marcus Mariota set to start in his place.

stories.headline: TEXAS A&M CRATERS TO NO. 23 AFTER UPSET LOSS TO KENTUCKY AS OLE MISS SURGES TO NO. 4
stories.body: Texas A&M fell 15 spots to No. 23 after an unranked Kentucky squad beat the Aggies 31-21, while Ole Miss jumped four spots to No. 4 behind Trinidad Chambliss' 32-24 win over Lane Kiffin's LSU, and Texas held onto No. 1 with a 30-6 win over UTSA following last week's upset of Ohio State.

deepDive.title: How a Falling Oil Price Can Do the Fed's Work for It
content: Today's brief has a built-in tension: the Fed hiked rates 25 bps last week to a restrictive 3.75%-4.00% and signaled it isn't done, yet Treasury yields eased and stocks ripped higher on the same day oil cratered toward $92. That's not a contradiction — it's a reminder that monetary policy doesn't operate in isolation from commodity markets. A sharp, geopolitically driven drop in oil can move the inflation outlook almost as much as a rate decision, and today's price action shows traders treating cheaper crude as a partial substitute for further Fed tightening.

The mechanism runs through the CPI basket in two stages. The direct effect is mechanical: energy components, gasoline chief among them, make up several percentage points of headline CPI, so a double-digit percentage decline in crude flows almost immediately into a lower gasoline price index and a lower headline inflation print within a month or two. The indirect effect is slower and broader: cheaper oil lowers transportation, shipping, and plastics-and-chemicals input costs across the economy, gradually showing up in core goods prices over two to three quarters as producers pass savings through their supply chains.

What gets missed is how much this dynamic can decouple headline inflation from the underlying trend the Fed actually cares about. In the 2014-2015 oil crash, WTI fell from roughly $100 to under $30, and headline CPI briefly went negative even as core CPI, which strips out food and energy, stayed comfortably positive. The Fed had to explicitly talk markets through that gap, arguing the energy-driven softness in headline numbers was not evidence that underlying price pressure had disappeared — which is exactly why the Fed's preferred gauge is core PCE rather than headline CPI.

That history is the lens for today's setup. If Iran-driven oil relief holds, it buys the Fed room to soften its hiking rhetoric without formally reversing course, since headline inflation optics will look better even if core price pressure hasn't budged — which is likely why the 10-year eased today despite last week's hawkish hike. The number to watch from here isn't the next headline CPI print; it's whether core PCE cooperates and whether oil's drop survives past this week's diplomatic momentum, since a snapback in crude would erase the disinflationary assist markets are pricing in right now.
